name: Stroke Rehabilitation
summary: High-repetition, task-specific practice, strength, aerobic activity and functional training are central, with safety and individual neurological deficits guiding dosage.

redFlags: New neurological deterioration suggesting recurrent stroke
Acute DVT or severe medical instability
firstSteps: Assess transfers, sitting/standing balance, walking, upper-limb function, sensation, neglect and communication needs.
Check blood pressure, heart rate and medical stability.
Choose one mobility goal and one upper-limb/ADL goal.

stages.label: Start: assess and set up
stages.goal: Prioritize meaningful tasks and high-quality repetition rather than passive movement alone.
do: Assess transfers, sitting/standing balance, walking, upper-limb function, sensation, neglect and communication needs.
Check blood pressure, heart rate and medical stability.
Choose one mobility goal and one upper-limb/ADL goal.

stages.label: Treat: build capacity
stages.goal: Dose practice according to cardiovascular tolerance, fatigue, cognition and motor severity.
do: Constraint or intensive upper-limb practice in appropriate patients
dose: Sit-to-stand: repeated task practice, e.g. 2–5 sets of 5–10 reps as tolerated.
Walking: frequent bouts accumulating meaningful steps; increase duration/speed gradually.
Strength training: 2–3 sets × 6–15 reps for available muscle groups.
Reaching/grasp practice: high repetition with task variation.
Aerobic training: moderate intensity when medically appropriate.
moveOn: Increase repetitions, task complexity, speed and environmental challenge

stages.label: Progress and self-manage
stages.goal: Use manual facilitation only to help the patient perform the task more successfully.
when: Increase repetitions, task complexity, speed and environmental challenge
dose: Increase repetitions, reduce assistance and increase task complexity.
Progress from blocked practice to variable real-world practice.

logic: Prioritize meaningful tasks and high-quality repetition rather than passive movement alone.
Dose practice according to cardiovascular tolerance, fatigue, cognition and motor severity.
Use manual facilitation only to help the patient perform the task more successfully.
manual: Soft-tissue or joint mobilization for secondary pain/stiffness
Avoid treating tone as a problem that can simply be 'released' manually
Use guided handling to improve alignment or allow successful movement practice.
Mobilize painful/stiff joints only when there is a true secondary musculoskeletal restriction.
Do not describe spasticity as something that can simply be 'released' permanently by massage.
modalities: NMES/FES may assist selected motor goals
Positioning and splinting only when clinically indicated
Passive modalities should not replace task practice
FES/NMES can support selected motor goals when appropriately indicated.
Use orthoses/positioning only for a defined goal.
progression: Increase repetitions, task complexity, speed and environmental challenge
Increase repetitions, reduce assistance and increase task complexity.
Progress from blocked practice to variable real-world practice.
mistakes: Too much passive ROM and too little task practice.
Not measuring walking speed or function over time.
education: Explain neuroplasticity as repeated meaningful practice.
Train caregivers in assistance that promotes independence rather than doing everything for the patient.
escalation: Urgent medical response for new stroke-like symptoms
Coordinate with multidisciplinary team for swallowing, cognition, speech, spasticity and medical issues
